## Why This Matters

In 2006 Netflix offered **\$1,000,000** to anyone who could beat its in-house recommender,
Cinematch, by 10% — measured on a hundred million movie ratings. The contest ran three years, drew
thousands of teams, and popularized a whole family of algorithms. That is how much a *better
suggestion* is worth.

It is not just Netflix. The "For You" feed on TikTok, "Discover Weekly" on Spotify, "Customers who
bought this..." on Amazon, the next video on YouTube — each is a recommender deciding, out of
millions of options, the handful you actually see. Recommendation is one of the highest-leverage
applications of data science in industry, and the surprising part is how far you get with tools you
already have: the **dot product** and **cosine similarity** from L18, the **mean-centered cosine**
that was Pearson's $r$ in L19, and the **latent-factor** view of PCA from L20.

## The Core Idea

A recommender estimates how much a **user** would like an **item** they have not seen. Given users
$U$ and items $I$, we want a function

$$f : U \times I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$$

that scores every (user, item) pair, so we can rank the unseen items and show the top few. All we
start with is the **user-item matrix** $R$, where $R_{ui}$ is the rating user $u$ gave item $i$ — and
almost all of it is missing, because nobody rates more than a sliver of everything.

![A 60-by-80 corner of the MovieLens user-item matrix drawn as a grid. Dark-blue cells mark the few user-movie pairs that have a rating; the overwhelming majority are pale (unrated). A few columns and rows are noticeably denser, marking popular movies and very active users. The full matrix is 943 by 1682 and 93.7 percent empty.](assets/l22_sparsity.png)

That emptiness — **sparsity** — is the central challenge. Recommendation is the art of filling in a
mostly blank matrix from its few known entries.

## Two Kinds of Signal: Explicit vs. Implicit Feedback

Where do the entries come from?

- **Explicit feedback** — the user deliberately rates: 5 stars, a thumbs-up, a like. Honest and
  clear, but rare; most people never rate anything.
- **Implicit feedback** — behavior the system observes: clicks, watch time, purchases, skips,
  re-watches. Abundant but noisy (a click is not love; a long watch might be background noise).

Most real systems run mostly on implicit feedback, simply because there is so much more of it.

## The Family of Approaches

There is no single "recommender algorithm." There is a family, each leaning on a different kind of
information. This lesson builds the first row; **L23 takes up the rest** (content, knowledge,
demographic, hybrid) and how to choose between them.

| Approach | Core idea | Needs | New-user cold start |
|----------|-----------|-------|---------------------|
| **Collaborative filtering** *(this lesson)* | "People (or items) similar to this one..." | a ratings matrix | **fails** — no ratings yet |
| **Content-based** *(L23)* | "More items like the ones you liked" | item features (e.g. genres) | needs a few likes first |
| **Demographic** *(L23)* | "People in your group liked..." | user attributes (age, region) | **works** — no ratings needed |
| **Knowledge-based** *(L23)* | "You said you want X, Y, Z" | explicit rules / user input | **works** — asks directly |
| **Hybrid** *(L23)* | combine several of the above | mix | depends on the mix |

## Collaborative Filtering

**Collaborative filtering** is the workhorse, and the one you build in the lab. It ignores *what* an
item is and looks only at the pattern of ratings: find users who rated movies the way you did, then
recommend what they liked. "Rated the way you did" is measured with **cosine similarity** between two
rating vectors $a$ and $b$ — the very operation from L18:

$$\cos(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \, \lVert b \rVert}$$

One refinement matters. Before comparing, we **mean-center** each user (subtract their average), so a
generous 5-everything rater and a stingy 3-everything rater can still look similar — they agree on
*shape*, not absolute level. Mean-centering and then taking the cosine is exactly the **Pearson
correlation** $r$ you built in L19: collaborative filtering is correlation between rating vectors.

It comes in two flavors:

- **User-user** — "users like you also enjoyed...". Find the user's nearest neighbors, then score
  each unseen movie by the neighbors' similarity-weighted ratings.
- **Item-item** — "because you liked this movie...". Compute similarity between *movies* (across the
  rating columns); recommend movies close to the ones the user already liked. Item-item is usually
  steadier — a movie's rating pattern changes far more slowly than a person's taste — and it is what
  Amazon's classic "customers who bought..." shipped.

A caution you will see in the lab: a movie rated by only a handful of people can show a *spuriously*
high similarity to anything by chance. Real systems require a **minimum number of ratings** before
trusting a similarity — a standard guard against those flukes.

## The Cold-Start Problem

::: {.callout-important title="Cold start: the new-user, new-item wall"}
Collaborative filtering needs a *history* to work — so it is helpless for a **brand-new user** (no
ratings to find neighbors from) and a **brand-new item** (no one has rated it yet). This is the
**cold-start problem**, and it is the hard limit of everything in this lesson. The fixes lean on
approaches that do *not* need a rating history — demographic and knowledge-based for new users,
content-based for new items. **That is exactly what L23 is about.**
:::

## Matrix Factorization: the Same Latent Space as PCA

Comparing whole rating vectors works, but it is shallow. The idea that won the Netflix Prize goes
deeper: assume a handful of **latent factors** — hidden "taste" dimensions like *action vs. romance*
or *blockbuster vs. arthouse* — explain the ratings. Each user gets a short vector $p_u$ (how much
they want each factor); each movie gets a short vector $q_i$ (how much it has each factor); and the
predicted rating is their **dot product**:

$$\hat{R}_{ui} \approx p_u^\top q_i, \qquad R \approx P\,Q^\top$$

That second form should look familiar. In **L18** the motivating example for **matrix times matrix**
was *"a users-by-factors table times a factors-by-movies table gives predicted ratings"* — this is
that example, now real. And the *idea* is **L20's PCA**: there, PCA embedded penguins into a 2D space
where each axis was a learned combination of measurements. Here we embed *users and movies* into a
shared $K$-dimensional taste space, and a movie's coordinates are exactly the kind of "loadings" you
read off a PCA.

![Three small heatmaps side by side. The first, P, is a tall four-users-by-two-factors table (factors labeled action and romance). The second, Q-transpose, is a two-factors-by-five-movies table. The third, their matrix product P times Q-transpose, is a four-users-by-five-movies table of predicted match scores: the action fan scores highest on Die Hard, the romance fan highest on the Notebook (with the rom-com next), and the user who likes both scores highest on a movie that has both factors.](assets/l22_mf_factors.png)

The one difference from PCA: the ratings matrix is mostly empty, so we cannot run plain PCA on it. We
**learn** $P$ and $Q$ by gradient descent on the observed ratings only — the lab does this from
scratch, in about twenty lines.

## What's Next: Does It Actually Work?

You will *generate* recommendations in the lab — personalized top-N lists, similar-movie lists, a
factorized prediction matrix. They will look plausible. But "looks plausible" is not a measurement.
**How do we know a recommender is any good?** Hide some ratings, predict them, and score the error
(RMSE/MAE) — and beyond predicting ratings, how well does the *ranking* match what users actually
want? That is **L23**: the other approaches *and* how to evaluate all of them, including the famous
ladder where each idea beats the last.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why not just recommend the most popular items?"** Popularity is a fine *baseline* and a reasonable
cold-start default, but it is identical for everyone — no personalization — and it buries the long
tail of niche items that make a catalog valuable. The whole point of a recommender is to beat "most
popular."

**"Is this machine learning?"** Yes — matrix factorization is a model fit by gradient descent, and
modern systems stack deep networks on top. But notice you get most of the way with similarity and
averages. Sophistication is earned, not assumed.

**"Does more data just solve it?"** It helps, but the hard parts — cold start, implicit-feedback
noise, fairness, and the feedback loop where recommendations shape the very behavior you learn from —
are not fixed by volume alone.

## Ethics & Privacy

Recommenders are powerful enough to be dangerous. The Netflix Prize dataset was "anonymized," yet
researchers re-identified users by cross-referencing public movie reviews — a landmark privacy
lesson. Beyond privacy, recommenders can trap people in **filter bubbles**, amplify outrage because
it maximizes watch time, and quietly encode bias from who rated what. These are not side issues;
**Unit VIII** takes up data governance and ethics directly.

## Key Takeaways

- A recommender estimates $f : U \times I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ from a **sparse** user-item matrix;
  sparsity is the core challenge.
- The approach **family**: collaborative (this lesson), content-based, demographic, knowledge-based,
  hybrid (L23) — each leans on different information.
- **Collaborative filtering** turns the crowd into personalization via **cosine similarity** on
  mean-centered ratings — which is L19's Pearson $r$ between rating vectors; it comes user-user and
  item-item.
- **Cold start** breaks collaborative filtering for new users and items — the bridge to L23.
- **Matrix factorization** learns latent user/item vectors: L18's matrix product and L20's PCA idea,
  applied to recommendation — and it is what the Netflix Prize crowned.

## Cheat-sheet

| Task | Idea |
|---|---|
| Build the ratings matrix | `ratings.pivot(index="user", columns="item", values="rating")`, then `.reindex` to the full user/item range |
| Mean-center a user | subtract that user's average over rated movies |
| User/item similarity | cosine of the mean-centered vectors (= L19 Pearson $r$) |
| Score an unseen movie | neighbors' similarity-weighted (centered) ratings, add the user mean back |
| Latent-factor prediction | $\hat{R} = P\,Q^\top$ (L18 matrix product; learn $P,Q$ by gradient descent) |
